utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone present in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, Boris Zorko, our new intern Mr. Morrison, and my name is Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence is ready to call the next witness, Mr. Sinisa Borovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness make the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. For the record, could you state your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Sinisa Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of November, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The municipality Ivanica, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, at the outset, I will tell you what I've already mentioned in your proofing. First of all, I would like to ask you whether you have ever testified before this Tribunal or any other court?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I have never testified before this Tribunal or any other court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The two of us speak the same language and it needs to be interpreted, hence, I'd like to ask you to pause following each of my questions before you provide an answer. You can see the screen with the text before you and perhaps you can refer to that. Once the cursor stops, you can start responding. There's no need to focus on that heavily, it's simply enough for you to wait a moment. I'll start with your CV. First of all, I don't know whether you prefer me to address you with "General" or "Professor," in any case, it seems more natural for me to address you as General during this testimony. Do you know when you graduated from the military academy?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the military technical academy in Zagreb in July 1968. The first degree, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will go through your duties you had as you moved through your career with the JNA and the VJ. As for your military education, in addition to the military academy, do you hold any other higher military degrees?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the military technical academy, I completed the military staff academy of the then-JNA, as well as a foreign languages school degree. I also hold a PhD.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About the PhD?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It's in military sciences. It was undertaken for the needs of the military. It had to do with the systems of technical security at the level of the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, do you have any civilian degrees, so to say?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I hold a bachelor's degree in shipbuilding and machine technical sciences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat this last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to you repeat your last answer, sir. They didn't hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a PhD degree with the shipbuilding and machine technical science school in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it in the same specialty?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was with the centre for multidisciplinary studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now rush through certain parts of your military career. Perhaps you can simply confirm that between 1975 and 1991, your duty was that of a lecturer at the technical educational centre of land forces in Zagreb and you held different positions there?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Between the 2nd of December, 1974, and up until 1991, I worked for the technical educational centre of land forces in Zagreb. I moved from assistant to professor to full professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you mainly dealt with technical security?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was the chair of the department in charge of technical security and organic science.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that while you were in Zagreb, you attended a PhD course in December 1989 in Poland. Actually, it was a post-doctoral degree. For the needs of these proceedings can you tell us what was your post-doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The post-doctoral thesis was a system of technical security of armed forces. That is to say, national armies and the armies of the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following that, in March 19 -- excuse me, in August 1991, you moved to the General Staff of the then-JNA. First you were head or chief of electronic equipment administration, and shortly after you became assistant chief of the operational staff affairs administration with the technical administration of General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in Belgrade because I was elected professor at the higher military school in Belgrade for methodology and research in military sciences, but given that there was no work for me at that moment in time due to the situation, I was assigned to the administration with the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the subsequent period up to your retirement, did you remain in the school as a lecturer, those duties running concurrently to those with the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Between 1974 and today I have always taught, I have never skipped a single semester and I have always seen myself primarily as a lecturer, as a professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness I believe said that he saw himself primarily as a professor. It wasn't clear to me what the English transcript said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between July 1992 and in the subsequent period, you were appointed head of technical services of the sector for land forces with the 1st Army headquarters in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you returned to the General Staff of what by that time became the Army of Yugoslavia in December of 1993 where you were appointed chief and deputy chief of the administration for technical equipment of the land forces with the same sector of the General Staff, that is to say, the logistics sector of the Army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was appointed chief of the technical equipment administration and deputy chief in the logistical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In November, you were appointed chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remained in that position until December 1996 when you went to work for the centre of high military educational institutions and, shortly after, you became the dean or the head of that centre. First because there was a vacancy in the establishment and later on your placement was confirmed by decree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The previous chief became ill sometime before that and by the time I arrived, he was no longer in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at page 6, line 6, when you say, "In November, you were appointed chief of the office of the Chief of the General Staff," are you referring to November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, November 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, then you must mention the year each time because the last year you had mentioned was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I have but I was probably hasty and spoke too quickly again. I apologise in any case. Then it must be Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, General, between March 1999, and you were appointed chief of the technical administration in charge of the logistical -- in the logistical sector [Realtime transcript read in error "centre"] of the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, your last position with the VJ prior to retirement was in December 2000 when you were appointed assistant to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ for the communications sector IT, electronic and something else, I always forget the acronym, what does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It is the communications, IT, electronics, and anti-electronic warfare sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have a clarification for the record, and for Mr. Lukic's benefit I'm referring to page 7, line 2, the answer says "logistical centre." I'm not sure if that was intended to be sector as opposed to centre, and perhaps the witness can clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please state what your position when you were appointed assistant, what is that unit -- organisational unit of the General Staff of the VJ called?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The technical administration which also had the technical service of the land forces, air force, technical administration, and navy technical administration, I was appointed assistant to the chief of the armed forces sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What organisational unit is this in?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You retired in September 2001 by presidential decree. Who was the then-president of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostunica, Dr. Vojislav Kostunica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we have to look at another area and that's your professorial work. We've already heard that you did post-doctoral studies, but what was your doctoral dissertation in mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: My doctoral thesis was called "Expert system for the control of the technical support system."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, are you perhaps a member of some academy of fine arts and science?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm a full-time member of the academy of engineering sciences of Serbia and Montenegro and a full-time member of the academy of the sciences of the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question regarding your career. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm currently a professor at the academy for diplomacy and security. I lecture in the subject of the theory of decision-making and I'm the dean of the chair for the management of small and medium-sized enterprises in Belgrade where I lecture in the subject of business management and quantitative methods in decision-making, operation research, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your civilian life after retirement, did you occupy any positions?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: After retirement I was assistant and deputy general director of the petroleum industry of Serbia for four years, and then, I was director general of the HIP petrochemicals in Pancevo. After that, I was advisor to the general director of the petroleum industry of Serbia and advisor to the president of the board of management.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say NIS, that would mean what?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The petroleum industry of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I occupied another position, in fact. When Mr. Tadic was defence minister, I was executive director in the defence ministry of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "Mr. Tadic," you mean the president of the Republic of Serbia today?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was then defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was after what we call the democratic changes when Milosevic was replaced; right?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will run through your career chronologically and the facts that you are going to testify to, and we are going to focus on the time when you were part of the cabinet of the General Staff of the army. But before that, when you returned from Warsaw and came to the General Staff of the then-JNA, what was the prevailing sentiment among the officers cadre in the JNA concerning the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I was personally surprised because most generals thought that Yugoslavia or at least the bulk of Yugoslavia will survive and be preserved, a view that I did not share. I was looking at things from a distance, from Warsaw, and I realised that the forces that wanted disintegration were stronger and that it wouldn't happen as the officers thought. But the military brass did not see it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your professorial and officer's career did you deal with strategic research?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: From the time when I assistant professor onwards, I continuously dealt with strategic research especially in the centre for the methodology of research and the methodology of military skills including the unit for research. I continuously co-operated with that centre, and when I became commander of the centre of military schools, I gave assignments to that institute and worked together with them on assessments and projects of interest to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you use the services of that centre even at the time when you occupied the position of Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I respected their work and I knew personally the researchers, and when we needed to check certain information and analyse and provide quantitative support, I did co-operate with that institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have now a couple of questions about your activities when you were part of the technical administration in 1991 and later until 1994, practically, although that includes a stint in the 1st Army. What were your duties while you were in the technical administration in 1991 and early 1992 until the Army of Yugoslavia was established?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: That had to do with the development of the service, building up the organisation, information, infrastructure of the service, modernisation of the service, establishing a new administration for a new army, changing the system of compartmentalising of materiel reserves of the army, repair shops and centres, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was your superior at that time when you are in the technical administration?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: First General Djukic and then General Ratko Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean Djordje Djukic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in that technical administration in this line of work, in view of the fact that the VJ had started to evacuate from the territory first of Slovenia and then Croatia and move to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? What kind of challenge was it from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a challenge because the JNA was in the process of disappearing. All the documents had to be redrafted because the previous documents had been drafted for a large country and a large army. All this had to be reworked. Many units were coming to the territory of Serbia that had not been there before and they had not been within our jurisdiction, they were within the jurisdiction of the army. So there was a lot of work in re-organising and administering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that many units were coming, what was to be done with these units?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: They were mainly arriving with their own moveable reserves and supplies that they had as part of their own kits and combat sets. All that had to be admitted and identified, then stored and registered in our system. Most often it didn't even arrive. It was deposited at some field locations that had been prepared for the army in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of a challenge, if any, did the officers cadre arriving newly to Serbia represent?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a problem because their status had been regulated in the territories of the republics that had seceded, not in the Republic of Serbia. It had to be regulated now in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to deal in greater depth with this topic. The technical and repair institute in the system of the former SFRY, to whom were they subordinated and what they were a part of?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The old Yugoslav People's Army had five repair institutes, maintenance institutes. Three of them were for machinery; Bregana, on the border between Slovenia and Croatia; then Hadzici, in the region of Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina; and Travnik in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The technical maintenance institute of Cacak in Serbia and the technical maintenance institute Kragujevac in Serbia, they were subordinated to the technical administration of the Yugoslav People's Army. In addition, the Yugoslav People's Army also had naval and air force technical maintenance institutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already heard some testimony about that, so I won't go into detail. After the establishment of the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ, did anything change in this chain of subordination of technical maintenance institutes? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, only the maintenance institutes in Cacak and Kragujevac remained at the disposal of the Army of Yugoslavia. They were originally established with large capacities to service a large JNA, and for the Army of Yugoslavia their peacetime capacity was too large.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: That means that the plan of general maintenance of combat equipment of the Army of Yugoslavia that was to be implemented by the maintenance institute did not envisage the use of all capacities of the maintenance institutes, and that's why they were transformed into military profit-making institutions which allocated certain capacities to act as profit-making enterprises on the market, either providing services to other entities, such as the Jugopetrol company, or they were supposed to go through conversion and move into civilian activities, which they did. For instance, the institute in Kragujevac which dealt with ammunition had a good carpentry shop producing packaging for ammunition, but they started to produce casings, honey-making packaging, watches, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Who approves the plan of maintenance for the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The technical administration for the technical maintenance institute in Cacak. It was the section for machinery and for the munitions, explosives, and lethal assets section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who approves that plan?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The chief of technical administration. According to the general plan of assignments of the Army of Yugoslavia, every assignment has its number, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't go into that. Once the plan is approved by the chief of technical administration, funds need to be provided. And who decides ultimately how many -- how much funding is to be allocated for the technical maintenance institutes?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It's the finance and development administration of the Army of Yugoslavia that decides on the allocation of funding based on the specific assignment in general maintenance plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where do the funds come from?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: From the budget administration of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the technical administration in its plans and in the approval of its plans ever cited requirements to finance anything related to Republika Srpska or the Army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned military profit-making enterprises within those institute, that means they can decide how they will use those free capacities independently of the army plans?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they able to provide their capacities, personnel, and services to the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of the RSK if they wanted?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it was financially profitable, yes, and if they were sure they could collect money for these services.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who would be the one to decide on concluding such a deal?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Either the institute itself or an administrative body which was called the association of maintenance institutes. It was just an umbrella organisation linking these two institutes for purposes of administration to know what they were being used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If they decided to do that, did they need the approval the administration or any other body of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not need any approval. They issued semi and annual analyses on the use of their capacity and the balance or the state of their finances, and any profits found its way to the republic and federal budgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this period which I refer to as the break-up of the country between 1991 and 1993, did you go to any of the maintenance and repair institutes in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if so, for what reason?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I -- towards the technical and repair institute in Travnik with the late General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Ratko Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me conclude the answer. And the maintenance and repair institute in Hadzici near Sarajevo. The management of both institutes were upset with the developments in the country. They wanted the chief of administration of the General Staff to tell them what the assessment and estimates were about any further development of the institutes in those locations, and in general what our position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was my assessment even back then that it was to be our last visit to those institutes. I openly stated that until further notice, until the final stage of the break-up, we were no longer going to finance any development projects of the institute, or institutes. If they remain under the jurisdiction of the General Staff finally, and under our administration, then any financing and development projects were to be picked up from where they were left off. In case of the institutes becoming parts of other states, they were to, of course, negotiate their fate in accordance with the newly created situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At line 16, page 1 [sic] I believe that the witness said the break-up of the country, or excuse me, or maybe he meant to say the final outcome of the break-up. The final result, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the equipment of the three institutes in Travnik, Hadzici, and Sarajevo, the ones you toured after the JNA withdrew?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: All of the institute's equipment remained there, mainly heavy machinery. The perhaps the only things that could be moved were some light tool sets and they were then taken to Serbia. I only know that from the institute in Travnik, some special gauging measurement units were brought on board a vehicle into Serbia and that is something the other two institutes did not have. All other equipment remained in the same locations. There was no possibility to extract it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you in the technical administration -- well, let me ask you this first, although we didn't touch upon it during proofing, but when did this visit take place in relation to the establishment of the FRY in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was just before the winter and the conditions were sufficiently poor to make our return from Sarajevo difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the technical administration have information about fuel levels and reserves of the JNA in the whole of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened with those fuel reserves once the JNA left Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The fuel kept in stationary tanks which were of the capacity between 20- and 70.000 tonnes remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. These are large reserves which simply could not be moved. The units only brought back their unit or troop reserves, what they could carry in their tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who took possession of those stationary fuel reserves, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I do. The paramilitary forces. They first went for the storages and warehouses because they were poorly defended. Once the JNA withdrew, storage crews were usually attacked or eventually allowed to pull out while leaving their reserves behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "paramilitary forces," what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The then-forces of the Croatian National Guard, and any Serb and Muslim forces that were outside the framework of the state. We considered them all to be paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on to the next topic concerning this period of the transformation of the armed forces. A moment ago you said you worked on organisation and formation of the newly established army in your technical administration. I also wanted to ask you whether you participated in the general plan making process of organisation of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I participated in general terms in all types of re-organisation, starting with General Mirkovic, who was the chief at the outset, onwards. I was one of the very few organisational science professors with the General Staff, and as such, I took part in the work of all those teams. That period continued until or during the tenure of Mr. Tadic, who is now president and was at the time defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that a new army model was being created, can you explain that to us as laymen, what does that mean in terms of organisation?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In order to come up with an organisational structure of all branches and services of the army, as well as to economise and reach optimal levels, strategic levels, one needs to include a number of criteria, such as financial criteria, demographic criteria, as well as to plan the development of specific units and institutions of the VJ. First of all, we need to deal with their defence structures, then finances, materiel, personnel issues, locations, et cetera. Only a person dealing with all those can appreciate the magnitude of such an organisational plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis the former JNA in terms of organising active-duty personnel, what were your problems when planning for the establishment of this new VJ?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: From the outset, we were trying to come up with an army that would match the size of the state. We faced very serious personnel issues rather than professional issues. We created -- we were in the process of creation of a smaller army which simply did not have enough positions for all of the personnel who eventually ended up in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that I heard you say that you were creating a new army and a new state; is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify the transcript. The problem you mentioned -- well, can you explain to the Chamber what it means to have an organisational establishment plan of an army? What does it mean in terms of a single officer, for example?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, his military specialty needs to be taken into account with the VJ. It also needs to take into account one's professional background, establishment rank, pay category or salary category, i.e., all status issues which had do with the work and life of an army member. It all needs to be included in our establishment plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once such a structure is put in place of the VJ, is it then known for each and every member of the VJ where that person is supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that person has a unique place in that establishment system. He is assigned his own special numbers and files.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another brief topic before we move to the office of the Chief of General Staff and your own activities there, and those are the international sanctions imposed by a resolution of the Security Council of the UN in the summer of 1992 against Yugoslavia. From your professional points of view, how did these international sanctions impact on your activities?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: They had a number of consequences. We had to create a model of preparing decisions for delivering equipment to the army against the background of an international embargo and international blockade, and that had to include all the know-how about high criteria-ranking and high criteria decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "we" who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Myself and Mrs. Dragana Becejski, a PhD, I was in the examiners commission when she defended her thesis, and she worked in the General Staff office providing IT support and she's now a regular professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: We received a model of recommendations, we published it in our press and then we modified it before publishing it abroad because this was -- these were professional papers. It was concentrated on a model of decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: We published it in the civilian magazine in 1994. It was called "Kvalitet" [phoen], this magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, what was your conclusion in researching this model? What was the point, the gist of it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It would take awhile if I were to explain that. With the embargo and the blockade and the sanctions, there always remained certain interests, as shown by other research, that prevented the embargo from being implemented 100 per cent, and the recommendation was, after analysing many alternatives, that suppliers used before the blockade should continue to be used finding other ways, other channels to bypass the embargo. We had to find new ways and the actual routes had to be found by the suppliers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From your knowledge, who was it that broke the embargo at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The embargo was violated by all the countries in our region; Croatia, the Muslim Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the states that co-operated with them and with Serbia both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move to the point when you became Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of General Staff. That was in December 1994, as we've heard. First of all, did you want to be appointed to that post, and how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I did not wish that post, although, I knew General Perisic, we had worked together in the Pula garrison as second lieutenants and lieutenants. Still, I did not want to work in the office and to deal with protocol, receiving guests, dealing with residences and villas. I wanted to be a professor and do my own professional work. However, General Ratko Milovanovic, whom I held in very high esteem both as a superior officer and a very clever, bright general, invited me one Thursday to talk to General Perisic. The general apparently found it very difficult to work with the staff at the office that he found there and he needed help in organising or re-organising the work of that office. That Thursday I could not accept it and General Perisic gave me a dead-line until the following Monday to think about it. That Monday I received another call from General Milovanovic and he asked me what my decision was. I said I decided not to accept. He showed me a notebook and told me I shouldn't complicate things because they had a session of the collegium the day before and I was already appointed Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of General Staff, that I should go and see the general, there would be a little treat at the office, et cetera. That's the way it usually goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I would like to look at D200 now, MFI. B/C/S page -- it's your tab 3, General. It's an order on the organisational units of the General Staff. D -- the English page is 1D2T -- sorry, 1D2-0972. And the B/C/S -- and the B/C/S is page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are having difficulty locating this document. I'm not sure we received -- we didn't receive this document, notification on this document. So if we could just have a minute or if we could get a copy of this document, it would be helpful to us. If there's a spare copy in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately I did not prepare English copies. I believe we announced this document. Yes, we did. I'm looking at the list of exhibits and we put it there. You see it on the screen now but I'll certainly wait for Mr. Harmon. Or perhaps we could take a break, Your Honours, now in order not to start with the document until Mr. Harmon has had time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we for a moment go back into private session, please, because of the document we just had admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may correct the record, it was our mistake but we really did not make this document available to the Prosecution, so I will not show it. I believe the witness will be able to answer my question even without the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Borovic, you don't have to look at the paper in front of you. I want to ask you, what are the basic duties of the Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: His basic duty is to cater to the Chief of the General Staff in all matters where the Chef de Cabinet can facilitate his work, to receive and send out mail, to receive visiting parties, support various facilities, take care of the security arrangements for the Chief of the General Staff in his travels and anywhere else, to prepare papers and presentations that the Chief of the General Staff is to make before the state bodies and various authorities, to follow up on tasks and duties that emanate from meetings, to take care of various villas and other facilities, to make security arrangements, to take care of the protocol, issue assignments to staff units and units immediately subordinated to the staff command, and to issue assignments to the guards brigade and the special units corps, to organise ceremonies on occasion or visits of delegations where such ceremonies are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the -- the office of the Chief of the General Staff has any staff functions?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of processing documents, analysing documents, and making summaries for the Chief of the General Staff, sorting out documents according to jurisdiction, documents that come into the office and are not addressed immediately to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who made up this office?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The Chef de Cabinet, the secretary of the Chef de Cabinet, the ADC of the Chief of the General Staff, deputy chief of the office that is deputy Chef de Cabinet, assistant of the Chef de Cabinet in charge of affairs pertaining to the deputy Chief of General Staff, the office of the general affairs, planning and general affairs, the protocol officer, the finance officer, the legal officer, data entry operators, archivists, drivers. I seem to remember there was more staff that I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are the duties of the assistant for legal and financial affairs?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The assistant for finance provides all the funding for travel and payments that fall within the purview of the Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff, including the payments of per diem to deputies, payment of expenses during visits of various delegations, funding for the development and appointment of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the assistant for legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: That was an advising -- an advisory duty in the office, and this person received all the documents that needed to be assessed from the legal point of view, including some documents that we received from the legal administration. They had to be reviewed for legality as did all the affairs of this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My next question, what kind of situation did you find when you first took up your duties at the office of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation I found was, in my opinion, rather primitive as far as IT and technical support is concerned, communications as well, including the inventory and the rolling stock. All that was below expectations, at least expectations of the office of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what was the first thing you set about doing?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I had to persuade my superior, who was of an ascetic disposition, that this had to change and that we had to equip the office with state-of-the-art technology communications equipment. We changed the rolling stock, that is the cars and vehicles available to the chief, later the entire furniture. And then we appointed the conference halls where sessions of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: And I forgot that we also had an information analyst as a member of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm interested in -- let me put it this way: What was the situation that you found there in terms of communication? What sort of communication did the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army have at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: He had civilian and military protected communications and he also had special communications at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did he have these special communication with?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: With the president of the republic, the president of the federal state, that is to say, with both presidents of the republics. I think he also had one with the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I don't think that he had one with the federal foreign affairs ministry. These were the special communication lines. And he had direct protected lines with all his subordinates, with the commanders of armies and with the commanders of independent units. That is to say, all the assistants within the General Staff. These were direct military lines. And of course, he had at his disposal civilian communication lines as well. He also had some so-called hot lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Do you remember, since you mentioned special communications lines, did he have a special communication line with the Ministry of Defence, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't. But it would be logical that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, please just tell us what you do remember. I'm not sure if it's necessary to clarify anything. When you say that he had special communications with the president of the federal state, who was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: While I was the chief of the office, it was Mr. Zoran Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were the presidents of the republic that he had special communication with?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was president Mr. Milo Djukanovic in Montenegro and it was Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, the president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it somebody else before Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It could have been Bulatovic. I'm not certain when was the time when they transferred from one duty to another, because this is what they used to do. They would just exchange positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to be clear, on page 31, in line 21, the witness said -- it's in the record "civilian military protection communication." He said "civilian and military protected communication lines." So there is no doubt there was separate civilian communication and military protected lines, so maybe just a comma should be inserted. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Chief of General Staff have a communication with the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had communication with the Chief of Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and he also -- I don't know if he had communication with all parts of the Serbian Krajina, but he did have communication with the top leadership while this area was still a republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And these communication lines, were they established during General Perisic's time or earlier, so before he assumed this position?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: They had existed earlier as well as the infrastructure, that was all in place already and nothing was done about this system of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "earlier," since when did these communications exist between the General Staff and, let me put it specifically, Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they existed as long as did the JNA because all places where the JNA existed were part of a communications network.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And since you assumed your position as Chef de Cabinet, was anything improved in terms of these communications?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No. That was not part of our competence. We didn't change anything and we did not even see these communication lines. They were not part of our integrated communications system. It was not up to us to maintain the equipment or the stationary communications centre or communication nodes. Resources were not planned for them so they were not repaired, adapted, modified, or maintained. The Yugoslav Army had its own communications system and its own maintenance of the communications system. I'm not sure how this worked in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that they were not part of the integral communications system, what do you mean, which communications?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, none of the communication lines which were part of the communications system but were in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Maybe some teams had to repair some of them but they were not within our system of checking, control, maintenance, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second. As you are a man who was in this line of work, what does it mean professionally, the maintenance of the communications systems, what does that imply?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It implies that resources are allocated from the budget according to duties and according to specific codes, that plans are made to maintain the system, to adapt it or modify it, repair the equipment, plans for renewal are made because there is equipment which becomes obsolete, new equipment is introduced and so on. So resources and capacities are allocated for this purpose. And then this operates as part of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Yugoslav Army in its plans maintained the communications systems of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: While I was Chef de Cabinet and also the chief of the communications department, we did not do that. We hardly had enough resources to maintain our own systems and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are the hot lines, can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: These are special telephone lines which the two collocutors have and which are not part of any procedure. So when you pick up the receiver, then the phone rings at the place of the other person with whom you have such a line established. And it is not used for regular communication. This is why they are called "hot lines." Only if necessary, such lines are activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were assigned to the position of Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of General Staff, did you take part in establishing any new hot lines and who with?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to reviving the hot line with the chief of the armed forces of Hungary, such a communication line was also established with the joint General Staff of the US Army. I was only present when a test call was placed when communication was established with, I think, Admiral Owen, who was the deputy of the joint chiefs of staff. But further on, I was not present during the establishment of this. Only when this first call was placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that, approximately? How long after the point in time when you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe during the last third of the time that I spent as Chef de Cabinet. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the information system, what did you introduce as something new to the work of the office?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I introduced everything that was necessary, the information system itself because there was no information system before, at the level of the staff and at the office, and it's like a current managerial information system. Something that's needed for the top leadership. Therefore we monitored everything from the printing of the daily newsletter about the situation in the units and the situation as regards the reserves and also monitoring resources, finances, documents, searches, everything that is necessary and that needs to operate. It's a managerial information system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would ask you a few questions about another segment of the office's activities, and that's the mail. What was the situation like -- but first let us explain to the Chamber and everyone in the courtroom, in terms of quantity, how much mail was received daily for the Chief of General Staff? On average, what were the various documents you would receive?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: On average, it would be between 50 and 300 documents of all kinds, from official documents to complaints and appeals that were private requests, and everything else that the Chief of General Staff would receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation that you found in terms of the daily mail when you assumed your position?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the first month while I worked with the previous Chef de Cabinet and was getting into stride in terms of the duties of the Chef de Cabinet, I found the situation in which the chief carried all the mail addressed to the office to the desk of the Chief of General Staff. I didn't change anything about that at the beginning for the first 40 days, but I believed that this was not rational, that it was exhausting and that it was just shifting responsibility from the lower levels upwards to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just stop here for a moment. When you said that it was not rational and this shifting of responsibility, what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not responsible to shift everything on to the Chief of General Staff. So whether a van would be given to the Red Cross to transfer children from one place to another, they would forward it to the Chief of General Staff for his approval, and in my evaluation, that made no sense that the military leadership should deal with that. The deputies and the assistants of independent administrations were the ones that should be doing that, because the climate was that no one dared to decide anything unless it was approved by the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your position about that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, my position was that there should be a very strict selection, and that whatever the assistants could do, that they should do it because that is why they existed, and only if there was something that the Chief of General Staff had to do or he was the only person who should be informed about that, that that was the only mail that should be forwarded to him. Or that the various chiefs and the assistant should process everything and then if the Chief of General Staff agrees, then that we should bring it to him and tell him, Well, this has passed all the procedures, so now you can sign it or you can refuse that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any resistance to the idea that the earlier procedure should be changed?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everyone resisted, from the chief to everybody else. The chief believed for awhile that we had cut him off from the public opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what did you do? In what did your new approach reflect?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we reviewed all the mail and then we sent it to the chiefs of independent administrations, to assistants, to the intelligence administration or the military diplomatic representatives, so we would only underline or put aside what was important for the Chief of General Staff. We only brought him the new information that he did not already -- that he was not already familiar with, so we knew what was -- what the office itself was familiar or unfamiliar with, so if something was repeated, then we wouldn't forward such information to him. We would just file that in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who personally informed the Chief of General Staff about the incoming mail which he did not need to deal with in more detail, and what was the procedure about the mail?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: While I was Chef de Cabinet, then the Deputy Chef de Cabinet, that was Colonel Borovic, did that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is requested to please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your last sentence is quite confusing in English translation. Can you just put it simply, who did that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Chef de Cabinet, that was Colonel at the time, Borovic, it says here General but that was me, I meant myself. But somehow I feel uncomfortable in saying, well, I was the one who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's much easier for us if that's the way we record it in our transcript, in the simplest terms possible.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: What kind of mail, what sort of documents were submitted to the Chief of General Staff through you on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, operative reports from the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just let us take it slowly and maybe go through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we could please see on the screen the document 9221 -- D221. I notified Mr. Harmon that it's one of the documents from the 65 ter Defence list, that's 657D. I just want to have a look at the form. It's the daily operations report which was produced by the duty team at the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just go through it a bit more slowly, please. We already had someone who testified about these documents here. Who were the -- all the persons who would receive such a document?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the operations administration, that is to say, the sector for operational affairs would receive it, then also the chief of the General Staff. And I am not sure if anyone else received it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Harmon has some information, but let me just inform the OTP that we submitted this document as 65 ter 657D. I won't dwell on this too long, I just wanted us to refer to the document briefly, and I apologise to the Prosecution if we provided this document under a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Such reports were sent when?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the morning when one gets in the office, the report had already been prepared and received by that time. We received such reports from the operational centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next part, then. What other types of reports were received daily by the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: There was always the bulletin containing information provided by the 2nd information administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have 65 ter 01086D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, it is your tab 10 but you'll also have it on the screen. We won't dwell on this one too long either. What is this and who drafts documents such as this one?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Such a document is drafted and forwarded to the Chief of General Staff by Colonel Krga, who was the chief of intelligence administration. This intelligence bulletin contained either daily information or was issued periodically as a result of analyses. It is then sent to the federal ministry, the General Staff, and independent administrations as well as the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see among the addressees the school centre. Did you also receive it later on?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It also says "destroy after reading." We always kept such documents in our archives in order to provide continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the next page of the document to see the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are, you said, periodical information; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was also daily information that was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go one step at a time. We see that this one is from March 1995. Without going in the contents, I believe the document speaks for itself. Perhaps peruse this page and the Chamber can be acquainted with a couple of things. I would particularly be interested in what follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose could we go to -- sorry, we should keep this in the English and go to the next page in the B/C/S version to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This chapter is called "Conclusions and Forecasts." Item 1 speaks of any estimates of potential foreign invasion. Who drafted or who created these estimates and in what sense was it important to the activities of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Conclusions and forecasts derived from our assessments arrived at at collegium briefings held once a week. On such occasions we usually drafted such conclusions and estimates, or maybe this particular one arrived from the intelligence administration. I can't see the entire contents, but I do know that we always followed the situation, and at collegium meetings, each of the assistants had to present their own information that would be then collated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can refer to it, it is in tab 10, and perhaps you can tell us who authored it.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: This particular one arrived from the intelligence administration of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please assign an exhibit number to this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D473. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to periodical reports of the intelligence administration, was there any daily information that found its way to the Chef de Cabinet and the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Daily we had the chief of the administration who would come to the office with new information. He always consulted with the office to see whether the office was in possession of any other information that was not included in the information they had prepared for the chief. It is always possible that we had some additional information. We also received coded telegrams, which would be then decoded in our office. We received those from our military attaches in our missions abroad. The 2nd administration also received such information, but we always double-checked that we had actually received the same telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the intelligence daily information that was provided, did the office of the Chief of General Staff receive any information from the information department of the VJ, and what was contained therein?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The chief received information from the administration -- information administration which was also brought up to date in terms of IT and procedure. He received reviews of information from the media that had to do with the VJ or were of VJ interest. They would then print out or issue what one may call a press clipping, although we didn't refer to it as such at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who visited the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ daily, and I don't want to lead you on this?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: When the chief was in his office, in addition to the Chef de Cabinet, he was also daily visited by the chief of the intelligence administration. It was General Dimitrijevic at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else visit him daily?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Krga who was the chief of the 2nd administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did their meetings with General Perisic vary in terms of content?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic usually went straight to the chief and he seldom visited the office before doing that. He would come to say hello because we were part of the same class at the military academy, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Krga?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: He would always go first to the office and then he would join the chief and General Aco Dimitrijevic during their briefings. After that, the Chef de Cabinet would bring the mail in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was you?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on we'll discuss the collegium meetings, but first let me ask you this: Outside the General Staff of the VJ, what offices were you in permanent or standing communication with?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The office of the Chief of General Staff was in standing contact with the military advisor to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was that at the time you were Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was General Krivosija first, and then from our office, Colonel Susic was assigned to that post and later promoted to the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the basic reasons for that contact? What were the topics discussed?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The military office of the president of the FRY prepared the agenda for any meetings of the National Security Council regarding all the issues mentioned vis-a-vis the army by the chef -- by the Chief of the General Staff. Then they also conveyed all orders by the president to us, or any demands the authorities had of the VJ. They also acted as a professional advisory body to the president because the president also had a similar civilian office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, you keep using the term the "president of the republic"?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I meant the president of Yugoslavia. The presidents of the republics within the Federation did not have their military offices, only the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had such an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to distinguish between the two, perhaps you should use the term "office of the president of Yugoslavia," or, for example, President Lilic's office as opposed to the office of President Milosevic, just to steer clear of any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a small correction for the transcript, Your Honours. I believe you understood that well, but in any case, line 20, page 44, the witness meant the Supreme Defence Council, for terminology sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- on that same line it says, "the military of the president of the FRY prepared the agenda for any meetings ..." Now, it can't be the military that prepares an agenda. Who was it supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify that as well. Who specifically sets the agenda for the Supreme Defence Council meetings? Whose authority was that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Of the president of the FRY, Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who prepared that materiel for him?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: When the Supreme Defence Council is sitting, it could also have on its agenda certain items which are not directly related to the ministry that were prepared by other ministries. But in any case, the agenda is set by the chief of the military office of Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have 65 ter document 00802D while we are on this topic. It is a decision on the establishment and scope of activity of the military office of the FRY president of January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see the title, and on the next page we'll see the decision itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to that page in both versions. We see the date. Could we briefly go to the last page to see who signed the document in both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Lilic signed it. This is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning this topic, could we see page 3 in both versions. Certain aspects of the scope of authority is referred to on that page. I'm trying to find the exact paragraph. It is also the third line in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Prepares the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council." It is item 3, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It also says: "Produces minutes of those sessions, submits excerpts from the minutes to the relevant organs and monitors the implementation of the conclusions."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've cleared that up, I believe. What is the next one, you needn't read it out loud because this will be part of the evidence, but I'm interested in particular in the last part. What does the last part of this bullet point mean in reality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph do you exactly mean? Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the fourth paragraph. It submits for signature and the proposals of decrees.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: What words does it begin with?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It actually ends with "having first considered their legal validity and prepare drafts of such statements itself, if necessary."

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The assistant for personnel, general and legal affairs, General Matovic, would prepare orders and decrees about promotion of officers that fell within the purview of the head of the military office of President Lilic and that would be submitted to the head of the office, and what fell within that purview were the ranks of generals. The military office would then take those decrees to the president, and the office of the Chief of General Staff did not receive these decrees, because these ranks were beyond their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another matter. It says the military office of the FRY president, and then its duties are described, having first considered their legal validity. And they prepare drafts of such documents themselves if necessary. My now question is, do you know if the military office of the FRY president had any legal officers qualified to review documents for legality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that in the civilian part of his office, the FRY president had people who were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this now for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D474. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the military office of the FRY president, which other office did you communicate with and how often?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: We communicated with the office of the president of Serbia, President Milosevic, we had frequent contacts with them and with Mr. Milosevic [as interpreted]. Less frequently but we were able to establish contact with the office of the president of Montenegro. And in its turn, the military office contacted as required the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They had no official communication with other offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 48, line 11, could you say again the last name of the Chef de Cabinet of the president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Goran Milinovic. Milinovic. I'm sure about the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Did you have communication, and how often, with the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'd forgotten about that. We had daily communication with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic, who is Goran Milinovic? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goran Milinovic, I will let the witness explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goran Milinovic was Chef de Cabinet of the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often did the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Lilic, visit you and the office of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic often visited the office of the Chief of the General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff himself, and army units in general. He was quite involved with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "often"?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Roughly twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judging by his contacts with you and other knowledge you may have, what was President Lilic's attitude to the General Staff and to General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was very correct, very fair. He had a lot of understanding for the problems of the army and he had every wish to assist the army and to strengthen the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often did the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, visit the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very rarely. Only exceptionally, in fact. When he pleased and several times he visited when the General Staff hosted the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often did you have occasion to meet President Milosevic aside from his visits to the General Staff and how many times did that happen at the time you were Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Quite often relative to his visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where would that be?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the residencies that we used for receiving guests in Karadjordjevo and in Dobanovci, at ceremonies and receptions, joint briefings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of President Milosevic towards the Army of Yugoslavia and General Perisic? Towards the army, in fact. I'll ask you about Perisic later.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was our pervasive impression that President Milosevic had an attitude towards the army that showed a lack of understanding and lack of trust in the military leadership and the army as an institution. It was certainly not a relationship of trust and co-operation on an equal footing.
