utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards the police compared to his attitude towards the army?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: He treated them much better, and that was obvious in terms of the equipment and facilities made available to the police. He favoured the police because the police belonged to the republic, and he had a certain aversion towards the army which was a federal institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to correct a slight error here. Page 50, line 4, the witness said "Karadjordjevo" and "Dobanovci," these are two locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are going to have it to spell them again for the stenographer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: K-a-r-a-d-j-o-r-d-j-e-v-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Interpreter. I think you were a little too fast for the stenographer. Can you spell that again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: K-a-r-a-d-j-o-r-d-j-e-v-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is the name of the other location, I better stay myself slowly. D-o-b-a-n-o-v-c-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, General, can we talk a bit about these two facilities, what are they and what is their connection to the office of the Chief the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: These were federal buildings intended for purposes of representation. They were not alone. There was also a villa at Tara and a villa in Meljinka and they were part of the property under the Chief of the General Staff. They were secured by the army. More specifically, the corps of special units. They were frequently used to house high-ranking delegations visiting the president of the FRY, Mr. Lilic, and the president of Serbia, and the presidents themselves spent time in these facilities. The Chief of the General Staff used them the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When there was an official visit to President Milosevic, independently of the military office, if someone wanted to see Milosevic and his office wanted to organise a meeting in one of these two buildings, what was the role of the office there?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The office of the president of the republic would send a request to the office of the Chief of the General Staff to have these buildings prepared to accommodate the high-ranking delegation in question, and that meant providing security arrangements, technical support, accommodation, recreation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. We need a clarification on page 50, lines 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To whom were these buildings subordinated?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: At that time the office of the Chief of the General Staff. Later they were subordinated to the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But they were not the property of the office of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I needed to clarify this for the record. Were you personally a participant in any meetings organised between President Milosevic and the leadership of Serbia with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never present or a member of the delegation at any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings after these gatherings?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I happened to be in that building after these meetings, I would be perhaps invited to stay for dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If meetings were organised there between some military delegations and General Perisic was present on one side, did you attend such meetings?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: If General Perisic attended military meetings, it was not a rule that I should be present too, but I would attend whenever he put me on the list and he requested my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you before who came when, and my next question would be, did General Mladic visit the office of the Chief of General Staff during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic did come to the office of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very seldom, and he never stayed long. He visited probably only in passing on his way to somewhere else. We would just send a car for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And whom did he see at the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: He would only see General Perisic. I don't know that he ever saw any other military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet with General Mladic on his visits to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three times. Once in the early days when I just came to the office of the General Staff, once when we hosted a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council, and a third time after a ceremony promoting cadets after graduation from military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you describe your meeting with General Mladic in the office of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have good memories of that meeting and if it's not really necessary, I would not like -- I don't know if you would insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You would like to do that now or would you like to do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would move to the subject of the collegium. What are the collegiums of the Chief of General Staff? And first of all, I will ask you who makes up the collegium of the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The collegium of the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army is made up of the Chief of General Staff, the Deputy Chief of General Staff, the sector chiefs who are simultaneously assistants to the Chief of General Staff, and the chiefs of independent administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often did the collegium meet?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: According to plan, it was periodical; that is to say, we had weekly meetings and outside of the plan as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to these regular collegiums and those held as necessary, were there any other collegiums and who would attend these meetings in such cases?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the regular meetings of the collegium, there were also the meetings of the so-called expanded collegium of the Chief of General Staff. In addition to the persons I named, now the army commanders would also attend as well as the commander of the navy, the commander of the RV and PVO, and units directly subordinated to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: They were held periodically and regularly that was twice a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, were such collegium meetings also held before you were appointed Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as the Chef de Cabinet of the Chief of General Staff, did you attend the collegium meetings once you were appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I attended the collegium meetings. I also had the right to participate in the discussion but I did not have the right to make any decisions. I could not vote on any issues and take part in decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "voting"?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it means approving of something, adopting something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you what was Perisic's position when decisions were taken in terms of the opinions of the collegium. When decisions needed to be taken, did he ask the members of the collegium for their opinion and did he respect and take into account their positions?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: General Perisic always allowed collegium members, he requested them to prepare and to state their views and when he was assessing the situation generally and within their own sectors, he always asked his associates to state their opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the collegium later on, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff when I was appointed chief of the high military school centre and I was at the same time an assistant of the Chief of General Staff in charge of education, training, and scientific research and publications within the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did every collegium of the Chief of General Staff have a specific form, and if so, how did one of these meetings look in terms of form?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just like everything else in the army, the collegium of the Chief of General Staff had a strict form. The Chief of General Staff would open the meeting, he would briefly say what the purpose was, and then he would give the floor to others according to certain order. First of all to General Dimitrijevic who was the chief of the security administration, then to General Krga who was chief of the intelligence administration, and finally to sector chiefs, the operational and staff sector and then others in their turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how did one collegium meeting end?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It would end by the Chief of General Staff summarising what was said and he would also issue tasks and set out dead-lines for implementing what was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when he issued the tasks at a collegium meeting, did that imply that he would issue these tasks orally or that later on it would be done in writing?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: He would issue the tasks orally but then we would all process them in writing for ourselves and turn them into plans and duties with specific dead-lines in a -- according to specific form where it would also be stated who the agents responsible for their implementation were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, once you came to the office did you introduce any novelties in terms of the technical form and protocol according to which these collegium meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think I did because we wanted to have collegium meetings without paperwork. We wanted to have visual presentations, and at a later stage, we also introduced audio recordings of the collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And for the internal needs of the office, did you do anything in terms of these collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: After listening to the audio recordings and after transcripts were typed up, the office always extracted from that an internal document which included the tasks issued during the collegium meetings. The office was supposed to monitor this, and at the beginning of each collegium meetings, the Chief of General Staff should be informed about what of these tasks which were issued during a previous meeting were in the meantime implemented or carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see P2891. It is a document which I didn't put on my list but during the proofing and in the proofing note I did inform Mr. Harmon of the facts contained in this document. And now, before presenting it, I received the approval of Mr. Harmon to present this document, which is an OTP exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, let us wait for the English version to appear on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this that we see on the screen right now? We can see that there is a stamp of the office of the Chief of General Staff in the upper-hand left corner of this document. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: This a document that was drafted after the audio recording of the collegium meeting was completed and this is a document which we would make by extracting some information for our internal needs in order to monitor the tasks and file this in our own archives so that we could always check exactly what is contained, and we would always give the reference to the audio recording and who processed it. We did it internally within our office and this was our copy that we used just for the needs of our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: For the needs of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say it was an internal document, can you say specifically for whose needs was this document drafted internally?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: For the office, for the Chief of General Staff and for other members of the office, for the assistant and the deputy of the office and the Chief of General Staff. So just for us, for internal use within our office. We needed it for the protocol and to see what tasks had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think that we have clarified that now. Now I'll ask you what was the task of the office of the Chief of General Staff when preparing a collegium meeting. What do the office staff do and who do you have to communicate with to do that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: For the regular periodically held meetings, the sector independent administration chiefs would submit to the office the questions which they wished to be included on the agenda of the collegium meetings. So these would be separate items on the agenda and there were always also the standard items such as the assessment of the security and intelligence and operational situation and then other items followed. These would be the issues proposed by the sector chiefs and then we would submit it for approval to the Chief of General Staff, and if he approved, then that would be included in the agenda for that specific agenda, and we would make a sort of plan of presentations in terms of the contents, the time that was needed, the presentations and so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I have concluded this topic, I would move to a different one now. General, did you have an opportunity to attend meetings with foreign military delegations, let me ask you such a general question, I mean with General Perisic, of course?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes, I did attend a number of meetings with foreign military representatives and I was in the company of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would focus on those which were held in the premises of the General Staff and then later on we might move to some other meeting as well. So let me ask you, first of all, did you have the chance to meet some highly ranking officers? Let me begin with the French army. Who do you remember as having visited the office and met with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: First there was General de Lapresle, and then later on he was Advisor de Lapresle. I saw him in both of these capacities. Then I also met General Janvier and officers who came with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to meet General Douin?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I did not meet General Douin because when General Douin landed at the airport, he did not wish to leave the aircraft and he did not come to the office, so this was resolved in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you in general terms, the meetings you had with de Lapresle and Janvier, what was the topic of discussion in these meetings and what did you learn about their positions expressed during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The principle was always that the general or the delegation which asked to be received by the Chief of General Staff would state the reason for their visit and their assessment of the situation in their zones of responsibility. They would also state their requests or their appeals or whatever they had to ask the Chief of the General Staff and the Yugoslav Army. They were always very decent in expressing the situation as they saw it and the goals of their mission, and they always acted in a military fashion, especially General Janvier. He always wanted to co-operate. He wanted to hear our opinion and to see what was possible, so trying to find common ground and perhaps trying to have some influence to make sure that everything can be done peacefully and that they can accomplish their own mission in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try and be more precise. What mission, what tasks, what influence?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Their mission was in the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they always discussed the situation in the field and how they see it as well as what their further plans were and what kind of assistance they expected from us as the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of any VJ assistance, what did they ask for?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they always wanted the chief to exert a certain degree of influence so that the parties to the conflict would see their role as neutral in order for them to be able to go about their task. In gist, that was it. They always asked for understanding and they wanted to see whether we could do something to influence the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To influence who in particular?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Usually to influence the leadership of Republika Srpska and the VRS. They didn't try to ask us to influence the conduct of the Muslim side, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was General Perisic's position during such meetings?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: General Perisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are getting into an area that is not described in the 65 ter summaries or are we getting into an area in the proofing notes. This is a new and more detailed area and that 65 ter and the proofing note merely mentions this witness was present with certain French officers and no further details are provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear with me, Your Honour. I believe that in the proofing notes, in the proofing notes, Your Honours, at page 2, we mentioned General Perisic's meetings with the French generals. That summary was received by the Chamber -- just a moment. In paragraph 18 -- sorry, paragraphs 17 and 18, therein we describe his meetings with certain people from France and Russia. We also explicitly stated that Janvier left a very good impression with the witness. During proofing it is not my obligation to disclose everything the witness said. I simply indicated the topic in the proofing note disclosed to Mr. Harmon, the topic of discussions with French representatives and I believe this suffices for him to prepare his cross-examination and that it was not at his detriment, especially having in mind that my examination-in-chief of this witness will take at least another day or two. And in that regard, I do not believe that this prevents Mr. Harmon from researching this fact any further and to put his own questions during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you're saying that you mentioned in your proofing note -- first of all, let me go back. Earlier you said the proofing notes at page 2 mentioned General Perisic's meeting with the French generals and that summary was received by the Chamber. Do you send proofing notes to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The summary is what you received but not the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understood Mr. Harmon's objection was that, according to him, in your proofing note you said that the witness was present when the French generals were there. In your response you are saying you mentioned to Mr. Harmon the topic of discussions with French representatives. Now, I don't have your proofing note before me so I don't know whether you said he was present when the French generals were there or whether you said there were discussions, so I'm not able to rule. And you see, I have a problem or the Chamber has a problem that -- with these objections that are raised based on a proofing note which is a document that we don't receive. I don't see how the Chamber can rule on such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out paragraph 18 of the proofing notes: [In English] "The witness was present at the meetings with Janvier, de Lapresle, Douin, Janvier, Douin. Janvier made an especially good impression on" him. Borovic was among the forming of the delegation visit in the Russia and Hungary, that's the other issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that that's the extent of the proofing note on -- in respect of these French generals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I don't want to revisit this but my objection was that there's no discussion in this proofing note of the content of that meeting other than there was a meeting and there was an impression formed. There's no further details provided in this proofing note or in any other proofing note that has been provided to us or summary by the Defence in respect of this -- these meetings with the French generals. That was the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, you are revisiting the point. Okay. So to say you don't want to revisit it, is not absolutely correct. Secondly, I think if proofing note mentions that there are discussions that are going to be heard, that were heard with the French generals, surely it's just not for them to be together that we want to know, we want to know what they talked about. And maybe you might have wanted to say to your colleague yes, you are talking about discussions with French generals in your proofing note but you are not telling us what was being discussed. Now, it looks like it's a little too late in the day to make that demand, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I received a proofing note on the 19th of September late in the afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can advise the Chamber of what can be confirmed by Mr. Harmon if we are still on this topic. Should I offer further arguments or should I go on with my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber did rule, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, my question was: What was General Perisic's position during such meetings with the French generals you've described?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Perisic always presented his position fairly and squarely to the French generals, and he always put things the way they were by saying that he had no control over the situation and that he was willing to use his personal influence to impact the situation, but that he cannot directly affect the behaviour of those in the field especially in the areas of responsibilities of certain generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were appointed Chef de Cabinet and later on, did you have occasion to learn of General Perisic's meetings with General Grachev, and did you meet with him as well?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that I saw General Grachev in Moscow and later on in the General Staff. When visits were prepared by the Chief of General Staff and the federal defence minister, Mr. Bulatovic, I would be acquainted with any previous meetings and relationships between the two armed forces. It was an obligation on the part of the office to be acquainted with the relationship, the types of co-operation, and to formulate our position for any such meetings, but this did not necessarily have to be adopted at the meeting itself. In any case, before any meetings, I was familiar with the position of foreign representatives, especially Mr. Grachev. As regards the issues discussed and the -- we discussed basically the same issues in Moscow with General Grachev and Russian defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was General Grachev's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: When I was in Moscow, General Grachev was still Chief of the General Staff, he may have been appointed minister by that time, but in any case, I think he was still in the position of chief because at that time there were in the middle of the situation with Grozny and it made the situation a bit more difficult. Although I may be mistaken, he may have been appointed minister by that time. I'm trying to recall who represented Russia and I think he was still Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Grozny?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: In Chechnya, there was a situation there and he discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter document 01327D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, it is tab 6 and we'll also have it on the screen. It is General Perisic's letter dated the 29th of July, 1994, sent to the minister of defence of the Russian Federation, General Grachev. The document speaks for itself. It has to do with the talks about adopting the group of the -- the plan of the Contact Group. Let's focus on the middle part of the letter. General Perisic states: "That is why I have invested and still am investing considerable effort to persuade my friend, General Ratko Mladic, to use his great authority to influence the political leadership of Republika Srpska to make them accept the Contact Group peace plan, believing that fair corrections would be made in the interest of the Serbian people. Nevertheless, it should be borne in mind that General Mladic's influence is limited because the political leadership of Republika Srpska will have the final say." This is what the letter states. Do you know what happened with the Contact Group plan in August 1994 and what was the position of the leadership and the military of Republika Srpska vis-a-vis the plan?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- I haven't been informed of that as the Chef de Cabinet, but I was one of the generals who was with the General Staff of the army and I know that the plan was rejected by the leadership of the RS. By that time, we had issued advice to have that accepted because the VRS had been exhausted by the time and there was no point to continue the war effort. But there was this constant lack of communication or disagreement between the VRS and the Serb leadership in the RS as well as the military and political leadership of Yugoslavia. Let me finish, please. We believed in the General Staff that our assessment of the situation was better, and that we had more information and better analytical ability as well as better connections with the world, and that we could see the situation far better than they could being -- because they were in the midst of the war. We also supported the measures of the international community. However, the leadership there believed that they were more familiar with the situation in the field and that we did not have sufficient understanding. This was the root of the conflicts or the misunderstanding, and I could basically see that General Mladic would not heed to General Perisic's advice and that he was basically acting out as the older acquaintance or friend of the two. We frequently analysed with General Perisic how we should put our case to them as to convince them that it was a better approach. In any case, the plan was finally rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say at page 67, line 24, you say the leadership did not accept the proposal, what leadership?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Of the RS. They never accepted the position of our leadership during the joint meetings held on the office premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are on this topic, I forgot to ask you something, actually it has to do with the last topic. Did anyone of the RS leadership visit the office and General Perisic? I have in mind the political leaders.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic was frequently in the office, and before Minister Buha travelled to Geneva, Buha, he came there for preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they come to see Perisic personally or did they come to the office?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: There was no reason for anyone to come to the office. They all went to see the chief if he was there. In any case, they also came to Belgrade because of some other issues. Civilians, for example, would come to the office and then would go on to see other people, and I know that Professor Koljevic met with Prince Karadjordjevic and that he frequently discussed matters with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have an exhibit number for this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D475. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we were -- while we are still with the Russians, were you part of any delegation on a visit to Moscow and you were visiting who?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were visiting Moscow and the delegation consisted of Minister Bulatovic, myself, I believe also the Chef de Cabinet of the chief, perhaps the Chef de Cabinet of the minister as well, although I'm not sure. It was not a large delegation. We had a definite set of issues to discuss. There was, of course, an interpreter and we were joined there by our envoy and the ambassador, Danilo Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately when that visit took place?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe in the latter part of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 01124D from the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document does not bear a date and if we look at the last page there's no signature either. Do you know anything about this document? Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was our draft made during preparations. Our minister would always carry a draft on such a visit whenever we initiated the visit. It's a draft of the agreement the way we see it and, of course, during the talks, it is further negotiated and harmonised and the final version is translated, but of course, you don't start such a visit without a draft. It was a working paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether some sort of agreement with the Russian Federation was ultimately signed during that visit?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the agreement as such was signed, but there was always an Official Note signed and a communique after our talks with Minister Grachev and the prime minister, Kozyrev.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see some writing, handwriting to the right of the stamp just below the line on which somebody would sign. Would that not be a signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my own reading of this, but perhaps the witness can tell us what that is below the stamp. If we can zoom in on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm addressing you because you are interpreted as having said: "There's no date and no signature either on this document."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, that's why I said this. If you look at the first page, it's just a kind of verification of the document, but if you look at the third -- in fact, this signature is not a signature of the negotiator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no control of the pages. I'm looking at the page that is before -- on the screen right now. I see some writing that looks like a signature. Is that not it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it isn't. If we can look at the third page. I know you are asking me -- but that agreement was not signed by the parties who were supposed to sign it. This is just a signature confirming that the document is authentic, like a confirmation of authenticity. But if you look at the last page, things become clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think let's turn to the witness because you are now testifying quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the third page then. Is this the third page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. In English it's page 3, but it's not page 3 in B/C/S. We need the next page in B/C/S. Next page in B/C/S. We need the end of the text. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can now explain all that we can see on the screen. Mr. Borovic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: This stamp and signature confirm on behalf of the person who let you have this document, that all the pages are there, but the signatures of the parties were to be affixed just below the lines that say "For the government of the Russian Federation, for the federal government of the SFRY." This was just written by the team that prepared this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the agreement had been concluded, where would the writing be? Would there be any blank spaces?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: There would be no blank spaces. You would see specific numbers in the line that says the agreement was done in such and such a place on such and such a date. These two lines would be filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that meeting in Moscow, do you remember what the positions of the parties were? Were the problems of the Republic of Serbian Krajina discussed?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: They were on the agenda, the problems concerning the Republic of Serbia of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I remember everything about that. I remember, and I'll tell you just about the finale. At the last meeting with the prime minister, Kozyrev, which lasted 30 minutes, Prime Minister Kozyrev explicitly put forward three questions. One, can the Republic of Serbian Krajina defend itself left to its own devices. Since the minister spoke Russian and I understand Russian, I understood what he said even before it was interpreted and we had our own position prepared. Our reply, the Republic of Serbian Krajina cannot defend itself left to its own devices. The second question was what [as interpreted] did the Army of Yugoslavia get involved in the conflict to protect the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Our answer again was that the Army of Yugoslavia would not interfere in the conflict of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and would not intervene militarily. And I think the third question was would the leadership of the Serbian Krajina come to some sort of agreement with the Republic of Croatia. I can't remember the exact wording of that question, but the three questions were very precise and we said no to all of them. And the minister concluded that the Republic of Serbian Krajina would be no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why was your position at the time and why did you say to Prime Minister Kozyrev of Russia that the Army of Yugoslavia would not get involved in the conflict in Krajina? What were your arguments?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Our overall position was that the Army of Yugoslavia would not get involved in any conflicts outside the borders of Yugoslavia. The JNA itself had never waged war outside its own territory. And the Army of Yugoslavia wasn't going to either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please get an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we can. Before we do, let me just understand your answer, Mr. Borovic. You say "the JNA itself had never waged war outside its own territory."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What year are we looking at hear? What year is this discussion that you are taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These discussions were in 1995, in Moscow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D476. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the General Staff of Hungary, and if so, when was that and who took part in that visit?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I was part of that delegation from the General Staff that visited the General Staff of Hungary, and it was in the town of Segedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up from the 65 ter list 10 -- sorry 01066D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, look at this document. Perhaps we should turn to page 3 to see who wrote it. Let's just wait for that page.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: You can see the initials. Biljana Borovic and Sinisa Majstorovic [as interpreted], that's a document I prepared for the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was signed by?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The chief, Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the previous pages. The document speaks for itself but what is the gist of it, who was it sent to, what was the purpose of this note?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: We prepare our own notes and the Hungarian side prepares its own, and before that we made a joint communique after the meeting. I can only confirm that whatever is written here is indeed so because I wrote it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: No one. It's our own document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: To whom was it addressed? Well, to our own authorities. We always had to report to the president of the Supreme Defence Council, that is, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We had to report after every visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what sense was it important for the position of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to co-operate with Hungary?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It's always important. Hungary is our neighbour. There is a large Hungarian minority in the north of Serbia. Hungary was at that time preparing to become a member state of NATO. It had military standards in its army that we were striving to match in the Army of Yugoslavia, and they were also very anxious to avoid any spillover of the conflicts in Croatia across their border, and that was our common interest, to follow-up on the situation, to monitor events, to have a good military co-operation, to have a direct communication without any special demands or plans, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the penultimate paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "Out of the areas of further bilateral co-operation, they expressed their wish that the existing telephone communication, the so-called hot line, would be maintained and made more reliable."

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: We already mentioned one type of hot line and they had misgivings about the security of this hot line because our communication systems were disrupted in certain areas. Some of them remained behind enemy lines and we promised to check on it and all the hot lines were indeed secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the last part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same page in B/C/S and in English we have to move to the next one. Concerning intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says "chief of intelligence." I'm especially interested in the last sentence. Was it customary for intelligence services of neighbouring countries to co-operate, and if so, why was it important?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Normally the countries that are not in conflict co-operate at the level of their intelligence services, especially if they have a good military co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D477. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear with me, Your Honours. I will change tack slightly. I will go back in terms of chronology and would return to certain topics at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about Operation Flash. We've heard evidence of it being underway in May 1995. And do you remember how that attack on Western Slavonia affected the position of the military leadership?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it had a negative impact for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which military leadership do you have in mind, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did those events impact on the position of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that the Army of Yugoslavia always saw such events, and this one in particular, as a further threat to the security of Yugoslavia and as something that would result in bringing the war conflict closer to our borders. This amounted to a new security situation which was more complex than the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter document 02176D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an intelligence bulletin of the 2nd administration of the General Staff of the VJ dated the 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe I asked you in -- during previous session about the author of this document. Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It came from our 2nd intelligence administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does the document say about Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it recognises the existing situation and offers further assessment of developments relative to or detrimental to the security of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me check if the paragraph I'm looking for in the English version is on this page. I believe it is the next page in the English version. One more page, please. The last paragraph, Your Honours. Before item 1.3, it is the middle of the page in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it says -- General, I'm reading it out now. It says: "On the other hand, the state and military leadership of the RSK burdened with internal conflicts, personal and other interests, had not undertaken everything necessary in order not to, firstly, fall for Croatian provocations and, secondly, to make all the preparations to successfully repel the aggression." Who did General Krga get this information from which he later entered into the bulletin?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: As any other intelligence service, his service also received information from his bodies and from the units he was in contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the next page in both versions, please. The next page in the B/C/S. It is page 4 so one more, sorry. Yes, this one. It is page 5 in the English. Sorry, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the first paragraph of 1.4, "Experiences." Whose assessment is this?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Also that of the 2nd administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we receive an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D478. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, in the summer of 1995, there seems to have been an incident in Markale market in Sarajevo, did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I did and so did the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you hear at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard that a shell landed at the market and that there were numerous victims. This initial information was followed by other information. Our intelligence administration immediately offered its assessment and the competent organs in the General Staff considered it, trying to pin-point the location where the shell had come from and what the reason for that was. As of the very beginning, it didn't seem to be a plausible explanation; that is, that the shell had arrived from the positions where the Serb forces were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. My first question is whether this was actually a controversy among the public as to the origin of the shell?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a controversial topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it also broached by the media?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was so in the media and intelligence services usually know how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have 65 ter document 01087D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again we have an intelligence bulletin, this one is number 28, and it is dated September 1995. Who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: It was offered by the 2nd administration of the General Staff and its chief, and by its chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here Markale 2 orchestrated by the USA and France, and some pieces of information are contained therein which speaks for themselves. At that time -- or, rather, let me put it in a more general way. Concerning different types of information you received, what information was more important and which were less important in your view?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The highest degree of authenticity and reliability was that offered by our 2nd administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you were to assess the quality of a certain piece of information and assign, say, grades to information coming from various sources, including the intelligence administration, how would you grade their information in situations such as this one?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, so as not to lecture here but I'll try to put it this way, if there is a piece of information coming from the 2nd administration and if I were to grade it with a 3, then if I were faced with a piece of information from the media, I would assign it a grade of .25.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much did you trust the media at the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: The army never trusted the media because they are prone to propaganda, sensationalism, and under the influence of those who control them and pay them. We, of course, considered those sources but we always tasked the 2nd administration to verify any information coming from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me correct something for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you graded security administration information with a 3, what grade would you give to media information?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: .25, in terms of importance of that information and its weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please repeat. Just the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again, Mr. Lukic. Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last two paragraphs, please read them and I'll have a question for you. Does what is stated therein reflect your recollection of what followed the incident at Markale concerning air-strikes on the positions of Bosnian Serbs? My question is this: Do you know what happened following the incident? In one sentence and then we'll discuss it further tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: I remember that no proper investigation was carried out and no credible expert opinion was provided by international experts. It was somewhat surprising to hear that the international community did not set up a team to investigate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it followed shortly afterwards by a military intervention?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Operation Deliberate Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document and I suggest we adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D479. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Borovic, we have not finished with your testimony. We cannot carry on for the day, we have to break for the day. You are still on the witness-stand, therefore you may not discuss the contents of this case with anybody, and least of all with the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the matter stands adjourned to tomorrow morning at 9.00, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
